To spurn someone or something means to reject it with contempt or scorn — not just to say "no," but to push it away with a sense of pride, disgust, or disdain. When you spurn something, you are making it clear that you consider it beneath you, unworthy of you, or deeply unwanted.

Think of it as a rejection that carries an extra emotional sting. It's the difference between politely declining a gift and throwing it back in someone's face.

Many words describe rejection — refuse, decline, reject, dismiss. But spurn is different in one important way: it always carries an attitude. There is pride, contempt, or scorn baked into it. When someone spurns something, they are not just saying "no thank you." They are saying "no, and I want nothing to do with this."

This is why spurn is often used in emotional, high-stakes situations — unrequited love, rejected peace offerings, dismissed advice from someone who cared. The word feels sharp and final. It conveys that the person doing the spurning had a strong, dismissive reaction — not a casual or reluctant one.

Spurn always has two roles: the person doing the rejecting, and the person (or thing) being rejected.

The person being spurned is usually someone who offered something sincerely — love, help, a proposal, advice, loyalty. The person doing the spurning pushes that offer away, often coldly or proudly. This is why being spurned hurts more than being simply rejected. It feels like a deliberate, contemptuous dismissal.

You can spurn a person, an offer, an idea, or an opportunity.

These will help you see how the word moves and feels in real use:

  • She spurned his romantic advances and walked away without a word. — She rejected him coldly and dismissively.
  • The proud king spurned the enemy's offer of peace, calling it an insult. — He rejected it with contempt.
  • He had worked hard to earn her trust, but she spurned every attempt he made. — She pushed away his efforts with disdain.
  • The young artist spurned his mentor's advice, convinced he knew better. — He dismissively brushed off the guidance.
  • They spurned the chance to settle the dispute peacefully, choosing conflict instead. — They rejected the opportunity with scorn or stubborn pride.

Notice how in every case, the rejection feels charged — it's never neutral or polite.

Understanding what a word doesn't mean is just as important as understanding what it does.

Spurn ≠ Decline. Declining is polite and gentle. "I'm afraid I must decline your invitation." There's no contempt there.

Spurn ≠ Refuse. Refusing is firm, but not necessarily emotional. "He refused to sign the contract." Clean, neutral.

Spurn ≠ Ignore. Ignoring means paying no attention. Spurning is an active rejection — you acknowledge the offer and push it away with attitude.

Spurn ≠ Reject (in casual use). "Reject" is a general, all-purpose word. "Spurn" is sharper, more emotional, and almost always implies that the thing being rejected deserved better treatment than it received.
The Emotional Texture of the Word

"Spurn" tends to appear in situations where the stakes are emotional. You'll find it in literature, formal writing, and serious speech more than in everyday casual conversation. If someone says "she spurned him," it paints a vivid picture — the cold shoulder, the wounded party, the proud dismisser.

The word also carries a slight moral undertone. Often, the reader or listener feels sympathy for the one who was spurned, because being spurned implies that something worthy — love, goodwill, an honest offer — was treated with undeserved contempt.
One-Line Summary to Lock It In

To spurn = to reject something with contempt or scorn, making it clear you find it unworthy or beneath you.

If you remember that single idea — rejection wrapped in contempt — you will never misuse or misunderstand this word.
